old_title: London snubbed in favour of Nairobi for 2029 World Athletics Championships
new_title: London snubbed in favour of Nairobi for 2029 World Athletics Championships
old_text:
London's bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships has ended in failure and heartbreak after it lost out to Nairobi. It marks an historic day for the Kenyan capital as it becomes the first African city to host the global championships.
Seb Coe, the World Athletics president, also announced that Munich would stage the 2031 event, saying it had "all the ingredients to be a spectacular world championships."
One source in the London team told the Guardian they were "gutted" at the news, given they felt they had a strong proposition. There will inevitably also be plenty of soul searching, given that London was seen widely as the frontrunner for 2029.
With hindsight, the long battle with West Ham over whether they would be granted permission to use the stadium in September 2029 did not help, while the sparse crowds on the opening days of the European championships in Birmingham last month was not ideal.
However, Lord Coe said that all four bids for the 2029 and 2031 championships, which also included Rome, had been outstanding. "This has not, as you can imagine, been an easy decision," Coe said.
"The council, the executive board, and our HQ leadership team have deliberated long and hard over the decision because there were four compelling propositions.
"Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. Nairobi has presented a compelling and an emotional bid. This is a fast-growing, dynamic, modern metropolis that serves as the economic, cultural, and political hub of East Africa.
"Kenya is one of the great athletics nations. The sport is woven into the fabric of the country, and athletes such as world gold medallists Faith Kipyegon, Vivian Cheruiyot, Eliud Kipchoge, Hellen Obiri and David Rudisha, as well as two-time Olympic champion Kip Keino, multiple world cross-country champion Paul Tergat and multiple world half-marathon champion Tegla Loroupe, have shaped the history of our sport.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment."
It is understood that Munich's presentation to the World Athletics' evaluation panel, which was tasked with recommending which cities should host the championships, was extraordinarily strong which made it the outstanding contender for the 2031.
"Germany has proved time and again that it is an outstanding and dependable host for major athletics events," Coe said. "Berlin 2009 remains one of the memorable editions of the world championships, and we have since seen tremendous support for the sport at the European championships in Berlin and Munich.
"The atmosphere in 2022 was exceptional and the attendance figures demonstrated the appetite that exists in the city and across Germany for major events."
The World Athletics Championships will next take place in Beijing on 10-19 September 2027, while both Nairobi 2029 and Munich 2031 will also take place in September at the climax at the end of the season.
new_text:
London's bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships has ended in failure after it lost out to Nairobi, the Kenyan capital which will now become the first African city to host the global championships.
Speaking at a press conference in Budapest the World Athletics president, Sebastian Coe, said the decision to go to Nairobi was historic and promised that it would stage a "groundbreaking championships".
While eyebrows will also be raised given that 318 elite Kenyan stars have been banned for violating anti-doping rules since the Athletics Integrity Unit was set up in 2017, a World Athletics spokesperson defended the decision, pointing out the Kenyan government had committed $5m (£3.7m) annually to anti-doping efforts.
"Kenya is much improved in this area, and we believe Nairobi hosting the world championships can act as a powerful catalyst in the Kenyan government's continued fight against doping," the spokesperson said. "It will put a spotlight on clean sport and galvanise the nation behind compliance."
As Nairobi and Munich, which was awarded the 2031 championships, celebrated, London was left licking its wounds.
One senior source in the London team, which had been seen widely as the frontrunner for 2029, told the Guardian they were "totally gutted".
Only over the weekend did some start to fear that their £45m bid, made up of £35m from the government and £10m from the mayor's office, might not get over the line. London believed it had a strong case , and the sight of around 60,000 fans watching track and field every night for a week was a compelling proposition.
Jack Buckner, the chief executive of UK Athletics, said: "We are deeply disappointed. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.
"Although today's announcement hasn't gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world's athletes love competing here and we'll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen."
In hindsight, the lengthy public battle with West Ham to get permission to use the stadium in September 2029 - which was settled only on the eve of the bid being submitted - was not ideal. The sparse crowds on the opening days of last month's European Athletics Championships in Birmingham perhaps did not help either.
However, the London 2027 team believed those factors were irrelevant, and it simply came down to a thirst in World Athletics for Kenya to host the championships, and the size of Nairobi's bid.
Lord Coe, though, stressed that there had been a range of factors at play. "Yes, of course, we see the historical, groundbreaking nature of taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa, but that alone is not the basis upon the decision," he said. "It was made across budgets, it was made across financial government guarantees, it was made across the growth potential of the sport. It was also grounded in some really serious analysis."
Coe also pushed back when he was reminded that going to Kenya would mean that Europe, which has the biggest fanbase for track and field, will have only staged one World Athletics Championships between one championship, in Budapest in 2023, between 2017 and 2031.
"Look, Europe is a heartland, and we openly accept that," he said. "It is in large part the breadbasket of our sport. But we do also have a responsibility to make sure that an international governing federation made up of well over 200 federations has the opportunity to be able to take our championships into areas that strategically we think will actually grow the footprint of our sport.
"And Munich 2031 is a European city. What it does allow us to do in the next three editions is to have our World Athletics Championships globally based: in Africa, in obviously Europe, and of course our next edition in Asia in 2027 [Beijing] next year."
